html:
The big picture

A program is a sequence of statements, and control structures decide which of them run and how often. There are two families. Branching chooses: the two-way if–else, the multiway if–elif–else and the value-based match statement, plus the conditional expression x if c else y that branches inside an expression. Repetition repeats: the while loop runs as long as a condition holds, the for loop iterates a loop variable over a sequence such as range. A loop's control can be interrupted by the jump statements break (leave the loop; the loop's else clause then does not run) and continue (skip to the next pass); structured programming uses them sparingly. assert checks conditions that must be true if the program is correct, and pass does nothing where a statement is required. The Nim game ties it all together, and the Graph.py toolbox makes loops visible as pictures.

Conditional statement (branching)

Two-way branching

Classical if statement:

if d == 0:
    print("Division forbidden!")
else:  # This part is optional
    quotient = x / d

Structogram on the slide: a condition box "d = 0?" with a "yes" column (error message) and a "no" column (quotient ← x / d).

Semantics

  • The condition (between if and :) is evaluated.
  • If it yields True, the body (statement(s) after :) is executed, and a possible else part is ignored.
  • Otherwise, the body is skipped up to the else part, and the statements in that body are executed. If there is no else part, nothing happens.
Connection

if/else was introduced in 3 Variables (prep course) with flowcharts. Here it's the "selection" building block of the Böhm–Jacopini result from 1 Foundations of Programming: sequence, selection and repetition are enough to write any algorithm. This chapter is the selection and repetition part.

Multiway branching

Example: translation of a numeric exam grade (Austria: 1–5) into a string.

Structogram: one case box "grade =" with columns 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, otherwise, setting text to "v.g.", "good", "sat.", "suf.", "fail" or an error, then "output text".

if grade == 1: text = "very good"
else:
    if grade == 2: text = "good"
    else:
        if grade == 3: text = "satisfactory"
        else:
            if grade == 4: text = "sufficient"
            else:
                if grade == 5: text = "fail"
                else:
                    text = "<invalid>"
print(text)

Deep nesting is hard to comprehend — in Python, there are nicer ways to formulate nested branchings…

Alternative 1: if–elif–else statement

if   grade == 1: text = "very good"
elif grade == 2: text = "good"
elif grade == 3: text = "satisfactory"
elif grade == 4: text = "sufficient"
elif grade == 5: text = "fail"
else:            text = "<invalid>"
print(text)

if–else is standard in most languages; if–elif–else is not so common (e.g. PHP, Ruby).

Best alternative for this kind of value-based multiway branching: match statement

match grade:
    case 1: text = "very good"
    case 2: text = "good"
    case 3: text = "satisfactory"
    case 4: text = "sufficient"
    case 5: text = "fail"
    case _: text = "<invalid>"
print(text)

(Margin note: here, always exactly one text = "..." is executed.)

Semantics

  • The expression between match and : is evaluated.
  • If its result is found as one of the case clauses, the corresponding statements are executed.
  • If no match is found, the statement(s) belonging to case _: are executed (if case _: does not exist, the control flow continues after the match statement).

In languages of the C family, match is called switch, with slightly weaker semantics.

Intuition — which form when?
  • if–else: exactly two ways.
  • if–elif–else: several ways decided by different conditions (if x < 0 … elif x < 10 …). The conditions are tried top to bottom and the first true one wins, so their order matters.
  • match: several ways decided by one value compared against fixed constants (grade 1–5, a menu choice, a command string). case _ is the catch-all, like the final else.

elif is just short for else: + a nested if, written on one level, which is why it reads so much better than the staircase above.

Common mistake — separate ifs instead of elif

Writing each case as its own if looks equivalent but isn't:

if score >= 50: grade = "pass"
if score >= 90: grade = "excellent"
else:           grade = "fail"

For score = 70, the first if sets "pass", then the second if is false, so its else overwrites it with "fail". The else only belongs to the if directly above it. With if … elif … else exactly one branch runs. (Also order matters in elif chains: test >= 90 before >= 50, or "excellent" is never reached.)

Conditional expression — branching inside an expression

Using if–else inside an expression. Assign the greater of x and y to z:

z = x if x > y else y

(Margin note: this is a rare example of a ternary expression: the ternary operator is if–else; the first operand is the value for the True case (x), the second the condition (x > y), and the third the value for the False case (y).)

Semantics

  • The value of the conditional expression is the first subexpression (x) if the condition after if yields True.
  • Otherwise, it is the second subexpression (after else, y).

In a conditional expression, the else part must not be omitted. An elif part is not allowed.

In languages of the C family, if–else is replaced by ?: and the condition comes first: z = x > y ? x : y;

Common mistake — the conditional expression binds weakest

if–else as an operator has the lowest precedence of all operators, so everything to its left belongs to the "true" value. 1 + 2 if False else 10 is (1 + 2) if False else 10, i.e. 10, not 1 + (2 if False else 10) = 11. When a conditional expression is part of a bigger expression, put it in parentheses: 1 + (2 if c else 10).

Repetition (iteration, loop)

while loop

# Outputs a line with vertical bars
n = number  # number of bars
while n > 0:
    print("|", end = "")
    n -= 1
print()

Structogram: n ← number; "While n > 0" box containing output "|" and n ← n – 1; then "Terminate output line".

(Margin note: end = "" tells print() not to end its output with an end-of-line character but with an empty string.)

Semantics

  • The condition (between while and :) is evaluated.
  • If it yields True, the loop body (statement(s) after :) is executed.
  • Then the condition is evaluated again, with the body possibly executed again, and so on, until the condition yields False.
  • Then the control flow continues after the loop.
  • (If the condition is already False in the beginning, the body is never executed.)

Example: program to calculate n! (»n factorial«)

# Computes n! = 1 x 2 x … x n
factorial: int = 1
n: int = int(input("N: "))
i: int = 2
while i <= n:
    factorial = factorial * i
    i += 1
print(n, "! =", factorial)
N: 5
5 ! = 120

(Margin note: here, the data type annotations are a matter of taste — all three variables are clearly of type int anyway.)

Trace for n = 5:

before iteration #ifactorialenter loop?
121yes
232yes
346yes
4524yes
56120no

The slide annotates the program with assertions (here specifically: a loop invariant): before the loop, and at the start of every pass,

\text{factorial} = \prod_{k=1}^{i-1} k,

and after the loop, where i = n + 1, this becomes

\text{factorial} = \prod_{k=1}^{n} k = n!.
Symbols
  • \prod_{k=1}^{m} k — the product 1 \cdot 2 \cdots m (capital pi = "product", like \sum for sums); an empty product (m = 0) is 1
  • i — the loop variable: the next factor to multiply in
  • n — the input; n! — "n factorial" = 1 \cdot 2 \cdots n, with 0! = 1
Why is a loop invariant useful?

A loop invariant is a statement that is true before the loop and stays true after every pass. Here: "factorial holds the product of all numbers below i". It starts true (i = 2: product of \{1\} is 1 ✓), each pass keeps it true (multiply by i, then increase i), and when the loop stops, i = n + 1, so factorial is the product up to n. That is a short proof that the loop computes n!, without testing every n. It also explains the edge cases: for n = 0 or 1 the loop never runs and factorial stays 1, which is correct (0! = 1! = 1).

for loop

A common pattern emerges here:

i = 2              # assigning an initial value to a control variable before starting the loop
while i <= n:      # control of the loop by the control variable (from ... to ...)
    factorial *= i # the loop statement(s) proper (»net loop body«)
    i += 1         # updating of the control variable for the next iteration

There is a separate loop version for this pattern:

for i in range(2, n+1):
    factorial *= i

(n+1: the control variable value one after the last one to be used.)

CallSequence
range(n)⟨0, 1, …, n-1⟩
range(start, n)⟨start, start+1, …, n-1⟩
range(start, n, step)⟨start, start+step, …⟩

Semantics

  • The function range(start, n) yields a sequence of numbers from start to n-1.
  • The loop variable (or control variable, i in this example) takes on these values one after another (it »iterates over the range«), executing the loop body for each value.

Later, we will see that we can iterate over all kinds of »iterable objects«.

Common mistake — the end of range is excluded

range(2, n) stops at n - 1. To include n you need range(2, n+1), as on the slide. Quick checks: range(5) is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (five numbers, starting at 0); range(10, 0, -3) is 10, 7, 4, 1; range(5, 2) is empty, because the default step +1 never reaches 2. The "stop is excluded" rule is the same one you know from slicing.

Intuition — while or for?

Use for when you know what to iterate over before the loop starts: a counted range, the characters of a string, the items of a list. Use while when the loop runs until something happens and you can't say in advance how often: until the user types nothing, until the matches are gone, until the ball… never (while True). Every for can be rewritten as a while (the four-line pattern above), but the for can't forget the update step, which is the classic cause of an endless while loop.

Factorial arbitrarily often — for and while loop

# Computes n! = 1 x 2 x … x n
# Exits when n ≤ 0
while (n := int(input("N: "))) > 0:
    factorial: int = 1
    for i in range(2, n+1):
        factorial *= i
    print(n, "! =", factorial)
# Computes n! = 1 x 2 x … x n
# Exits when the input is empty
while (userInput := input("N: ")) != "":
    n: int = int(userInput)
    factorial: int = 1
    for i in range(2, n+1):
        factorial *= i
    print(n, "! =", factorial)

Sample runs: both start N: 4 → 4 ! = 24, N: 8 → 8 ! = 40320. The first continues N: 11 → 11 ! = 39916800 and N: 0 ends it. The second accepts N: 0 → 0 ! = 1 (the slide prints it as 0!=1) and only an empty input ends it.

Common mistake — the walrus needs its parentheses

:= (the assignment expression from 3 Variables, Data Types and Expressions) has very low precedence. Without the parentheses, while n := int(input("N: ")) > 0: means n := (int(input(...)) > 0): n becomes True or False, not the number. Always write (name := expression) > 0.

Example program: the Nim game

Part I (initialisation)

# NIM Game: Minimal Variant
from random import random

matches: int = int(input("# matches: "))
max_take: int = 3
print("We play the game with", matches, "matches. We must take",
      "away between 1 and", max_take, "matches in each turn.")

# We “throw the dice” who may start:
computers_turn: bool = random() < 0.5  # function random() with 0 ≤ random() < 1
print("I" if computers_turn else "You", "start.")

(Program text in this colour — here from random import random — marks yet unexplained concepts. These will be dealt with later and must be used literally meanwhile.)

Part II (playing)

while matches > 0:  # Individual rounds
    for i in range(1, matches+1):
        print("|", end = "")
        if i % 5 == 0: print(" ", end="")
    print()
    if computers_turn:
        if matches <= max_take: take = matches  # Computer takes them all
        else:  # Standard case
            take = matches % (max_take+1)
            if take == 0: take = int(random() * max_take) + 1  # throw dice
        print("I take", take, "matches.")
    else:  # Human's turn
        take = int(input("Your turn (1-" + str(max_take) + "): "))
    matches -= take
    computers_turn = not computers_turn  # Change the active player
print("You" if computers_turn else "I", "won")

The slides show the structogram of the whole game next to the code: "While matches > 0" containing the output of the matches, the case "comp_turn?" with the computer's and the human's move, "matches ← matches – take" and "comp_turn ← ¬comp_turn"; after the loop, "comp_turn?" decides between "You won" and "I won".

Connection

This is the Nim program from 1 Foundations of Programming, now in real Python. Why matches % (max_take+1) is the winning move, and why the winner is printed with the flipped flag, is worked out there.

Worked example — tracing one round

17 matches, computer's turn, max_take = 3.

  1. Draw the matches: the for loop prints 17 bars, a space after every 5th (i % 5 == 0): ||||| ||||| ||||| ||.
  2. Choose the branch: computers_turn is True; 17 <= 3 is false → standard case.
  3. Compute the move: take = 17 % 4 = 1. Not 0, so no dice. Output I take 1 matches.
  4. Update the state: matches = 16 (a multiple of 4: the human is now in a losing position), computers_turn = False.
  5. Loop test: 16 > 0 → next round, human's turn.

»Emergency exit« from a loop

In the Nim example, let us enable the user to give up the game: if user_input == "quit", exit the game; otherwise take ← user_input. »Exiting the game« means leaving the loop and outputting that the user has given up (and, therefore, lost).

break statement — a rudimentary jump statement

Semantics: break exits the immediately surrounding loop.

break is a (very specific and therefore relatively harmless) jump statement, which should (in principle) be avoided in the sense of structured programming for loops. Simplified pattern for a workaround:

while B:                    while B and not C:
    …                           …
    if C:                       if not C:
        break      →                …
    …

However, in some cases break is actually quite practical — e.g. to exit from the middle of a rather long loop.

What was responsible for the termination of the loop?

If a loop may be exited from a position other than the loop header, it may be interesting to find out whether it has been exited by such an »emergency exit« or by the standard loop condition becoming False.

NIM example: after the loop, the system determines and prints the winner. If a message is already printed when the user quits, this final output may be redundant. If we only want to output the final message when the game has come to a normal end, we can do this in an else: clause of the loop.

# … (code as before)
while matches > 0:  # Individual rounds
    # … (code as before)
    if computers_turn:
        # … (code as before)
    else:  # Human's turn
        user_input: str = input("Your turn (1-"
                                + str(max_take) + "): ")
        if user_input == "quit":
            print("I won because you gave up.")
            break                       # also possible in for loops!
        take = int(userInput)
        # … (code as before)
else:  # This part is executed only if
       # the loop has terminated normally
    print("You" if computers_turn else "I", "won.")
# matches: 37
We play the game with 37 matches. We must take away between 1 and 3 matches in each turn.
You start.
||||| ||||| ||||| ||||| ||||| ||||| ||||| ||
Your turn (1-3): quit
I won because you gave up.

In most other languages there is no else clause for a loop, so one would have to re-check the while condition to find out what happened:

if matches > 0:
    # loop must have been terminated via break
Unclear (slide 91)

The code reads the input into user_input but then converts int(userInput) (camel case), a name that doesn't exist in this program: as printed, any input other than quit would raise a NameError. It should be take = int(user_input).

When exactly does a loop's else run?

The else block runs when the loop ends because its condition became false (while) or its sequence was used up (for), including the case where the body never ran at all. It is skipped only when the loop is left by break. So read else as "no break happened". Think of a search: for x in items: if found(x): break … else: print("not found") — the else is exactly the "searched everything, found nothing" case.

Common mistake — else of a loop ≠ else of an if

Indentation decides which statement an else belongs to. In the slide's code, the final else: is at the level of while, so it's the loop's else. Indent it one level deeper and it becomes the else of if computers_turn — a completely different program. Also, a loop's else does not mean "if the loop didn't run"; it runs after every normal end.

continue statement — another rudimentary jump statement (only in loops)

Semantics: continue exits the current pass of the immediately surrounding loop and continues at the loop head.

while (userInput := input("N: ")) != "":
    n: int = int(userInput)
    if n < 0:
        print("No negative numbers!")
        continue                  # also possible in for loops!
    factorial: int = 1
    for i in range(2, n+1, 1):
        factorial *= i
    print(n, "! =", factorial)

This is also a relatively harmless kind of jump statement, which should nevertheless be avoided in the sense of structured programming:

while B:                    while B:
    …                           …
    if C:                       if not C:
        continue   →                …
    …
Intuition — break vs continue

In a loop over the pages of a book: continue = "skip this page, go on with the next one"; break = "close the book". After continue, the loop condition is checked again (and in a for loop, the next value is taken); after break, the loop is over and its else is skipped.

assert statement — for checking assertions

Systematic testing of assertions helps to detect programming errors! If a condition, which is supposed to be always True due to logical considerations, turns out to be False, something must be wrong! Python supports the testing of assertions during program execution:

assert Assertion
assert Assertion, InformativeExpression

Semantics

  • None (like a comment), if assertion checking is disabled (console: python3 -O file).
  • When assertion checking is enabled, the logical expression Assertion is evaluated. If it yields True, nothing happens. Otherwise, the program is aborted (outputting InformativeExpression, if present).

(Corner sketch: x \leftarrow 3, y \leftarrow 4, z \leftarrow x \cdot y with the assertion x = 3, y = 4, z = 7, wrong, so the check fails.)

NIM game with assert

# … (code as before)
while matches > 0:  # Individual rounds
    # … (code as before)
    # Compute take, the number of matches to be taken away:
    if computers_turn:
        # … (code as before)
    else:  # Human's turn
        # … (code as before)
    assert take > 0, "take must be positive!"
    matches -= take
    computers_turn = not computers_turn
else:
    print("You" if computers_turn else "I", "won.")
# matches: 17
…
I take 1 matches.
||||| ||||| ||||| |
Your turn (1-3): 0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "NIM.py", line 36, in <module>
    assert take > 0, "take must be positive!"
AssertionError: take must be positive!

Note that it is not good programming practice if a user input can lead to an assertion error! User input must never lead to an assertion error!

Riddle: how can we improve the program to avoid this? Do it!

Worked example — one way to solve the riddle

Goal: the assertion should only catch programming errors, so invalid input must be handled before it. Replace the human's input line with a loop that asks again until the move is legal:

take = int(input("Your turn (1-" + str(max_take) + "): "))
while take < 1 or take > max_take or take > matches:
    print("Please take between 1 and", min(max_take, matches), "matches.")
    take = int(input("Your turn (1-" + str(max_take) + "): "))
  1. State the rule as a condition: a legal move is 1 \le take \le max_take and take \le matches.
  2. Loop while the rule is broken: the while condition is its negation.
  3. Ask again inside the loop, so the loop can end.

After this loop, take > 0 is guaranteed by the program's own logic, which is exactly what an assert is for. (Tested with inputs 0, 3 and 2 when 2 matches are left: the first two are rejected.) Non-numeric input like abc would still crash in int(); handling that needs exceptions, which come later.

Common mistake — assert for input checks

Assertions can be switched off (python3 -O), and then the check simply disappears. So an assert must never be the only thing protecting the program from bad input or bad data. Use if/while for things that can happen (wrong input), assert for things that cannot happen if your code is right.

Null statement

Does nothing — but is sometimes needed for syntactical reasons (when a statement is required and we do not want to do anything):

pass
Intuition

Python marks blocks only by indentation, so an empty block is impossible: if x > 0: followed by nothing is a syntax error. pass fills the hole, e.g. while you write the skeleton of a program and fill the branches in later.

Simple graphics — for more entertaining examples

The tiny toolbox Graph.py provided on the Moodle course page (use it as a »companion« file in your working directory) offers simple functions for drawing into a window:

import Graph  # Integrate the file Graph.py into the source code;
              # imported names are accessed via Graph.name(…)

Graph.create("A Match", 150, 200)       # Create a 150x200 window
Graph.set_pensize(10)                   # Make a thick pen
Graph.line(70, 0, 70, 130)              # (70/0) ➝ (70/130)
Graph.line(70, 130, 70, 150, "red")     # Draw a red line
Graph.show()  # Display the window (waiting until the ENTER key is hit)

The window is a »canvas« of 150 × 200 pixels with (0/0) in the lower left and (150/200) in the upper right; the result is a black match with a red head. Colour names: see below.

Intuition — "lower left" is unusual

Most graphics systems (including tkinter, on which Graph.py is built) put (0/0) in the upper left with y growing downwards. Graph.py flips this (its scale function computes window_height - …) so that you can draw with the maths convention: y grows upwards. With set_scale you can choose any coordinate range, e.g. -1 \dots 1 in both directions.

for loop example: random walk

Use random() to generate pseudo-random float numbers in the interval [0, 1) for ending points of consecutive line segments (next starting point = previous ending point):

import Graph
from random import random  # To use random() directly

Graph.create("Random Walk", 500, 500)
Graph.rectangle(0, 0, 500, 500)  # axes-parallel »Frame«
x1, y1 = 0, 0  # Starting point
for _ in range(200):  # 200 times (loop variable _ is »anonymous«)
    x2, y2 = random()*500, random()*500  # random() ∈ [0, 1)
    Graph.line(x1, y1, x2, y2)
    Graph.show(0.1)  # Update window and wait for 1/10 seconds
    x1, y1 = x2, y2  # Previous endpoint becomes new starting point
Graph.show()  # Update window and wait for the ENTER key

200 random line segments inside the frame.

for loop example: circle approximation

import Graph
from math import pi, cos, sin  # For direct usage

Graph.create("Approximate a Circle", 500, 500)
Graph.set_scale(-1, 1, -1, 1)
r: float = 0.9  # Radius (1.0 would be the unit circle filling the window entirely)
STEPS: int = 20  # Approximation resolution (number of polygon sides)
dPhi: float = 2*pi / STEPS  # Angle increment per step (360° / STEPS)
x1, y1 = r, 0  # Starting point: 3 o'clock = 0 degrees
phi: float = 0
for _ in range(STEPS):  # Cover 360° in radiants
    x2, y2 = r*cos(phi), r*sin(phi)  # Endpoint of line segment
    Graph.line(x1, y1, x2, y2)
    x1, y1 = x2, y2  # Previous endpoint becomes new starting point
    phi += dPhi
Graph.line(x1, y1, r, 0)  # Close the circle
Graph.show()

The slide recalls \sin\varphi = \frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \cos\varphi = \frac{\text{adjacent leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, so the point at angle \varphi on a circle of radius r is (r\cos\varphi,\ r\sin\varphi). With STEPS = 60 the polygon looks like a smooth circle; Graph.circle(0, 0, r) draws one directly.

STEPS = 20: a visible 20-gon.

Why does the polygon need a separate "close the circle" line?

Trace the loop: in the first pass, phi = 0, so the first point drawn to is (r, 0), the starting point itself (a zero-length line). The passes then visit the angles 0, \Delta\varphi, 2\Delta\varphi, \dots, 19\Delta\varphi, so the last point is one step before 360^\circ. The final Graph.line(x1, y1, r, 0) draws that missing 20th side back to 3 o'clock. Moving phi += dPhi to the start of the loop body would make the loop end exactly at 360^\circ and the extra line unnecessary.

Nested for loop example: spiral approximation

Riddle: implement these changes. Extend the circle program by adding another for loop around the circle-drawing loop, which runs, e.g., ten times. Starting with a small value, after each circle segment, slightly enlarge the radius: either additively (r += 0.0008) or multiplicatively (r *= 1.0023).

Left: 10 turns with the radius growing by a constant amount per segment (an Archimedean spiral, evenly spaced). Right: radius multiplied by 1.0023 per segment (a logarithmic spiral, tight in the centre).

Endless loop example: bouncing ball

import Graph
from random import random
from math import fabs  # fabs(x) = |x|

Graph.create("Bouncing Ball", 500, 500)
Graph.set_scale(-1, 1, -1, 1)
x, y = random(), random()              # Ball position
v_x, v_y = random()/15, random()/15    # Ball velocity (increment per step)
RADIUS = 0.05                          # Ball size
while True:  # Do forever (until window is closed): Update ball position and draw it
    if fabs(x + v_x) + RADIUS > 1.0:  # Hits right or left wall
        v_x = -v_x  # Invert horizontal component of movement
    if fabs(y + v_y) + RADIUS > 1.0:  # Hits upper or lower wall
        v_y = -v_y  # Invert horizontal component of movement
    x += v_x  # Move one step
    y += v_y
    Graph.clear()  # Clear old picture
    Graph.circle(x, y, RADIUS)
    Graph.show(0.01)

Riddle: implement the version with trace (the slide's picture actually shows it without trace: the ball's path as a criss-cross pattern, drawn when Graph.clear() is left out).

Unclear (slide 100)

The comment on v_y = -v_y says "Invert horizontal component of movement"; it is the vertical component (copied from the line above).

Intuition — reflection by flipping one sign

A ball hitting a vertical wall keeps its vertical speed and reverses its horizontal speed, like light in a mirror. So "bounce off the left/right wall" is just v_x = -v_x, and "bounce off the floor/ceiling" is v_y = -v_y. The test looks one step ahead (x + v_x) and includes the radius, so the ball turns before its edge would cross the wall at \pm 1.

Graph.create("Window Title", window_width, window_height)Creates a window with the given title, width and height (both in pixels)
Graph.set_scale(min_x, max_x, min_y, max_y)Establishes the user-defined coordinate system given
Graph.set_pensize(new_pensize)Changes the current pen thickness to new_pensize (in pixels) and returns the former setting
Graph.line(from_x, from_y, to_x, to_y [, pen_color])Draws a line from (from_x/from_y) to (to_x/to_y), using pen_color, if given
Graph.rectangle(lo_left_x, lo_left_y, up_right_x, up_right_y [, pen_color] [, fill_color])Draws an axes-parallel rectangle with the given lower left and upper right corners; pen colour pen_color if given, otherwise "black"; filled with fill_color if given
Graph.circle(center_x, center_y, radius [, pen_color] [, fill_color])Draws a circle with the given centre, using pen_color if given; filled with fill_color if given
Graph.text(lo_left_x, lo_left_y, "Text to print" [, pen_color])Writes the text starting at position lo_left, using pen_color if given
Graph.axes([pen_color])Draws the coordinate axes in grey or pen_color, if given
Graph.clear()Clears the window
Graph.show([seconds_waiting] | [prompt])Updates the window and pauses for the given number of seconds; with no argument or a prompt (str), waits for the user to hit ENTER
